steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptual Map of a Transformer  

0. 30-second “elevator” view  
   A transformer is a sequence-to-sequence model that learns to represent every element of an input sequence in the context of every other element via a mechanism called self-attention. That context-rich representation is then passed through simple feed-forward layers and stacked many times. Because attention looks at the entire sequence in parallel, transformers dispense with the recurrence used in RNNs and the fixed kernels used in CNNs, giving them both speed (parallelism) and flexible long-range reasoning ability.

----------------------------------------------------
1. Tokenisation & Embedding – “Give the model some pieces”  
• Text (or audio, image patches, etc.) is chopped into discrete tokens.  
• Each token is mapped to a high-dimensional vector (an embedding).  
• Because order matters, a positional signal (sine/cosine waves or learned vectors) is added or concatenated so that “cat sat” ≠ “sat cat”.

Result: a matrix X ∈ ℝ(seq_len × d_model) that contains the whole sentence as vectors.

----------------------------------------------------
2. Self-Attention – “Let every word look at every other word”  

Key idea: For every token we create three short learned projections:

   Query  = XW_Q  
   Key    = XW_K  
   Value  = XW_V  

For one head the attention operation is:
   scores   = (Query)(Key)ᵀ / √d_k        (similarity)  
   weights  = softmax(scores)             (normalize)  
   output   = weights · Value             (weighted sum)  

Interpretation  
• Query asks a question like “what in the sentence is relevant to me?”  
• Keys are potential answers; the dot-product measures relevance.  
• Values are the information that gets retrieved and blended.  
Thus each token’s new representation is a mixture of other tokens, weighted by learned relevance.

Multi-Head Attention  
Instead of one such operation, we run h of them in parallel, each with its own W_Q, W_K, W_V. Different heads can focus on syntactic roles, long-distance dependencies, sentiment cues, etc. Their outputs are concatenated and linearly remixed.

----------------------------------------------------
3. Add-&-Norm and Feed-Forward – “Stabilise and transform”  
For each layer:

   a) Multi-Head Attention  
   b) Add residual skip-connection to preserve information.  
   c) LayerNorm (standardise).  
   d) Position-wise Feed-Forward Network: two linear layers with a non-linearity (GELU/ReLU) applied to every position separately.  
   e) Another Add & LayerNorm.

Stacking N such layers forms the Encoder.  
The Decoder (for tasks like translation) adds:  
• Masked self-attention (tokens can’t peek at future tokens).  
• Cross-attention against the Encoder’s outputs (the decoder “reads” the source sentence).  

----------------------------------------------------
4. Training Objective – “Predict the next (sub)token”  
Most commonly, transformers are trained to maximise the probability of the correct next token given previous tokens and (in encoder-decoder) the source sequence. Cross-entropy loss and teacher forcing are used. Large-scale training on corpora (billions of tokens) yields general-purpose language models.

----------------------------------------------------
5. Why it Works – Intuitions  

Long-range context: Any token can attend to any other in one hop (O(1) path length vs O(n) for RNN).  

Parallelism: Attention on all positions is computed simultaneously on GPUs/TPUs.  

Expressivity: Multiple heads + deep stacking approximate many functions; attention can “route” information adaptively.  

Inductive bias: Unlike CNNs (local) and RNNs (sequential), attention is permutation-equivariant except for explicit positional encodings—this minimal bias lets the model learn patterns not fixed by architecture.

----------------------------------------------------
6. Variants & Extensions (names you might hear)  

• BERT – encoder-only, bidirectional masked-token objective.  
• GPT – decoder-only, causal attention, autoregressive.  
• T5, BART – encoder-decoder, denoising pretraining.  
• Vision Transformer (ViT) – image patches as tokens.  
• Performer, Longformer – sparse or kernelized attention for long sequences.  
• MoE (Mixture of Experts) – routes tokens to specialised feed-forward blocks.

----------------------------------------------------
7. Inference – “Generate or classify”  

Classification: pass sequence through encoder; read the special [CLS] token or pool over positions; attach a classifier.  

Generation: Feed prompt tokens, run masked attention, sample or beam-search the next token, append to input, repeat (autoregressive decoding).  

----------------------------------------------------
8. Computational Footprint  

Time: Self-attention is O(n²) in sequence length (major research topic to reduce).  
Space: Parameters grow with (layers × d_model²) plus embeddings.  
Compute: Primarily dense matrix multiplies—perfect for GPU/TPU.

----------------------------------------------------
9. One-sentence recap  

A transformer repeatedly lets every token ask, “Who else here matters to me?” (self-attention), gathers their information, passes the result through simple per-position neural layers, and stacks this process, producing rich context-aware representations that excel at language, vision, and beyond.
